title: Claude Code is accidentally exposing secrets all over GitHub
content:
Claude Code is leaking sensitive information on public GitHub instances thanks to a partial oversight in the way its settings files are handled. That’s the finding of AI security researchers at Apiiro, who discovered thousands of secrets, including database passwords, API tokens, and root logins, amid Claude Code settings files embedded in GitHub repositories.
The leak stems from the way Claude Code handles user approval for automated shell commands. When a user chooses the “Yes, and don’t ask again” option to approve running a command, that choice gets stored as part of a rule in the local “.claude/settings.local.json” file on the user’s computer. That rule is sometimes coded as a pattern, but the command itself is often written to that settings file as is, including any sensitive information that may be embedded within it.
This isn’t really a significant security issue if the settings file stays on the user’s local machine (assuming that machine doesn’t become compromised itself, of course). And Anthropic notes in its Claude Code documentation that this particular settings file gets added to the developer’s global .gitignore list, which usually prevents it from being shared publicly.
But that .gitignore setting isn’t reflected at the repo level, meaning the sensitive file can be uploaded accidentally if a repo is cloned to another machine or a folder becomes a repo later, for instance. In many cases, Claude Code itself will commit changes to the settings file without the user’s input, Apiiro writes.
Apiiro’s researchers found over 100,000 cases where Claude Code’s local settings file had been uploaded to a public GitHub repository. Of these, only about 1,100 from 63 different organizations contained secrets such as public API tokens, database passwords, or private keys. Even after these files are discovered and removed from a repository, the secrets can persist in forks of the original project if a GitHub user isn’t careful.

report.summary: Claude Code’s local settings file can capture approved shell commands with secrets and leak them through public GitHub repositories, researchers found.
report.background: AI coding assistants such as Claude Code can execute shell commands, install packages, and run tests on a developer’s machine. To reduce friction, they ask users to approve commands, with an option to remember the approval. That convenience is central to the leak: Claude Code stores remembered approvals in a local .claude/settings.local.json file, sometimes including the literal command and any secrets embedded in it. Anthropic says this file is placed in a global .gitignore, but global ignores are not automatically enforced at the repository level. If a project is cloned to another machine, or a folder is initialized as a Git repo later, the file can be committed and pushed. Claude Code may also commit settings changes itself. The incident reflects a broader tension in agentic development: tools that automate local workflows create new paths for credentials to end up in public code repositories, where secret-scanning and cleanup remain difficult.
key_points: When a developer approves a shell command with 'Yes, and don’t ask again,' Claude Code writes the approval into .claude/settings.local.json. The rule sometimes includes the full command, not just a pattern, so passwords, API tokens, or root logins embedded in that command are saved in plaintext in the settings file.

Apiiro found more than 100,000 public GitHub repositories containing Claude Code’s local settings file. About 1,100 files, from 63 organizations, held real secrets such as API tokens, database passwords, and private keys. The rest may still expose configuration details or indicate risky habits even when no live credential is present.

Anthropic says the settings file is added to the developer’s global .gitignore, which normally keeps it out of Git. But that ignore rule does not travel with a repository. If someone clones the repo to another machine, or turns an existing folder into a repo, the file can be committed and uploaded. Claude Code may also commit changes to it without user input.

Removing a leaked file from a repository does not fully erase the secret. Forks and clones can retain the file, and Git history may preserve it. Attackers and secret-scanning bots can find credentials in public repos quickly, so exposed tokens should be rotated, not just deleted.
report.impact: The leak is a trust test for agentic coding tools. Features designed to reduce approval fatigue can quietly create durable, plaintext records of sensitive commands, and global ignore rules are too weak a safeguard for teams. For developers, the practical lesson is that AI assistant settings are part of the attack surface: audit .claude directories, enforce repo-level ignores, scan history, and rotate any exposed credential. For the AI industry, it raises pressure to design safer defaults—redacting commands, storing approvals as scoped patterns, warning before commits, and integrating secret detection. Regular users may not run Claude Code, but they depend on services built with it; a leaked database password or API key can lead to breaches that affect them. The incident also shows that automation convenience must be balanced with secure-by-default configuration.
report.tools: To follow up, watch GitHub’s built-in secret scanning and push protection, and open-source scanners such as Gitleaks and TruffleHog for finding credentials in Git history and forks. Pre-commit hooks and git-secrets can block sensitive files before they are committed. Teams using Claude Code should add .claude/settings.local.json to repo-level .gitignore, audit existing repos, and consider secret managers or environment variables instead of inline credentials. Anthropic’s Claude Code documentation is worth monitoring for changes to settings-file handling.
